龍笛主要出現在日本雅樂（gagaku）合奏中，是雅樂「三管」之一，也用於演奏中國: The ryūteki appears mainly in Japanese gagaku ensembles, where it is one of the three winds, and it is also used for pieces in the Chinese style. In a gagaku ensemble the melody is usually carried by the hichiriki, and the ryūteki works with the other parts over a wider range; the opening of a piece is usually a ryūteki solo, played by the section leader. Modern works use the ryūteki too, for example Hans Werner Henze's El Cimarrón and the instrumentation of Karlheinz Stockhausen's Jahreslauf in its original gagaku ensemble version.
龍笛可能成型於唐代，經遣唐使傳入日本，並可能由中亞橫吹演變而來；今日僅見於日本。: The ryūteki probably took shape in the Tang dynasty and came to Japan with the embassies to Tang China, and it may have developed from Central Asian transverse flutes; today it is found only in Japan. Together with the nōkan and the shinobue it is regarded as the prototype of other Japanese transverse flutes, and it has long been used in gagaku as one of the three winds, above all for pieces in the Chinese style. From the end of the twentieth century the ryūteki entered modern works: Henze used it in El Cimarrón, and Stockhausen wrote for it in the gagaku ensemble version of Jahreslauf.
龍笛為氣鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs 編號 421.121.12，地: The ryūteki is an aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 421.121.12, from Japan. The source states only that the body is of bamboo and names madake in particular; the materials of the other parts, such as the blowing hole, the edges of the finger holes, any treatment of the bore, the joints and the decoration, are not recorded. It sounds by being blown across, and the source mentions neither a reed nor the material of any other sounding part, and it does not describe the material of the sounding body either.
龍笛音色明亮清澈，具有獨特的穿透力，帶有典雅的古典韻味。其音域寬廣，可演奏從低音: The ryūteki's timbre is bright and clear, with a distinctive penetration and an elegant classical air. Its range is broad, with rich layers from low to high, and in the high register especially its tone is sharp and soaring, highly expressive. It resonates in its own way: the bamboo fingerholes keep a warm quality in the tone while also keeping it bright. Beside the light agility of the shinobue the ryūteki is steadier and more solemn; beside the nōkan it is louder and more transparent. In Japanese gagaku it is known for its high, bright tone quality, and it often holds a dialogue with the other instruments; its timbre has great penetration and power to move, and it can be heard on its own within the ensemble as well as blending into it.

The ryūteki is a transverse bamboo aerophone used in Japanese gagaku, Hornbostel–Sachs 421.121.12. It has seven fingerholes, is about 40 cm long with an inner diameter of about 1.3 cm; the player covers the holes with the pads of the fingers without closing them completely, and by lifting a finger slightly makes half-hole and semitone changes. The ryūteki is one of the three winds of gagaku, and its range lies between those of the other two gagaku transverse flutes; it is often used for pieces in the Chinese style and the ancient Japanese style, and in an ensemble the opening solo is usually taken by the section leader.
